newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan unveils more deregulation but timing unclear.
newsitem.headline: Japan unveils more deregulation but timing unclear.

text.p: Japan on Friday announced a revised package of broad measures to deregulate the nation's economy but left the timing of many of the steps unclear.
"The package is aimed at deregulating rules which have been preventing a vigorous expansion of the economy and the creation of new business," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said.
He made the comment after the cabinet approved revisions to an action programme aimed at loosening red tape that foreign and domestic businesses say has been suffocating the economy.

The revised package is the final installment of a three-year programme containing 2,823 measures to deregulate areas such as financial services, communications, housing, distribution, transport, energy, labour and education.
The government admitted that only 890 of the measures were new. The rest had already been cited in some form by various government ministries.
"The plan is aimed at opening Japan to the rest of the world, and thus creating a free and fair economic society," the government said in a statement.
With many measures lacking a specific timetable, the government urged ministries to decide by the end of September when to implement the steps.

Specific measures in the package are designed to boost imports, closing gaps between prices in Japan and overseas and cutting the extra costs Japanese consumers pay as a result of excessive regulation.
Hashimoto has said his government is committed to cutting red tape to boost the fragile economy because its high-cost structure is making Japan less attractive to investors.

The package stresses the government's effort to shift its basic regulatory policy from that of meticulously creating numerous regulations and obligating firms to follow them to that of setting up basic rules and checking if firms are following the rules, a government official said.

The new parts of the revised package include steps to ease rules on foreign currency transactions in Tokyo and in Japanese stock markets. Stockbroking fees will be liberalised and restrictions on investment by Japan's hefty pension funds will be removed.

The package will also allow financial institutions to set up branches wherever they wish, introduce self-service petrol stations, and allow convenience stores to sell medical products. It will permit construction of higher buildings in city areas to create more living space, and ease rules on private job agencies -- a move aimed at reducing unemployment.
Other steps include dismantling regulations hindering firms from entering Japan's telecoms market.
The package also seeks to promote imports of housing materials, an apparent response by the government to demands by the United States -- Tokyo's biggest trading partner.

U.S. officials have repeatedly expressed disappointment at Tokyo's progress in deregulation. "Regulations lie at the heart of our market access problem with Japan," said Larry Greenwood, economic minister-counsellor at the U.S. embassy in Tokyo, earlier this month.
Analysts said the package left many points unresolved and would not have immediate positive effects on the economy due to the time it would take for the measures to be implemented.

The government will set up a new framework to promote deregulation beyond March 1998, when the current three-year plan ends, Management and Coordination Agency chief Kabun Muto was quoted by Jiji news agency as saying on Friday.
